title: EU AI Act Conformity Assessment Readiness: October 2026 Deadline — Council of AI Guide
context: 2026-09-15 engine cycle — The EU AI Act's high-risk AI system obligations (Title III, Chapters 2-3) became applicable on August 2, 2026. By October 2026, national market surveillance authorities must be operational, and notified bodies are expected to begin accepting conformity assessment applications. This seed page maps what deployers and providers need to have ready, and how the Council of AI measurement board provides the ongoing monitoring evidence that conformity assessment requires.
body: The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) is now the law of27 nations. After the prohibited practices provisions took effect in February 2025 and the general-purpose AI obligations in August 2025, the August 2, 2026 milestone brought the most commercially significant chapter into force: the full obligations for high-risk AI systems under Title III. Providers of high-risk AI systems must now maintain a quality management system (Article 17), keep technical documentation (Article 11), conduct conformity assessments (Article 43), register in the EU database (Article 49), and implement post-market monitoring (Article 72). Deployers must perform fundamental rights impact assessments (Article 27), ensure human oversight (Article 14), and monitor the system's operation continuously. The October 2026 milestone is when national market surveillance authorities are expected to begin active enforcement. Member states were required to designate at least one notifying authority and one market surveillance authority by this date. The European AI Office has published guidance on which conformity assessment procedures apply to which high-risk categories (Annex I, Category 1-8), and has clarified that self-assessment under Annex VI is permitted for most AI systems, with third-party assessment required only for biometric identification and emotion recognition systems. For the majority of high-risk AI deployers, the conformity assessment is self-assessment — but self-assessment under Article 43 is not 'trust us, we checked.' It requires documented evidence of ongoing risk management (Article 9), data governance (Article 10), technical documentation (Article 11), transparency (Article 13), human oversight (Article 14), and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity (Article 15). This is where the Council of AI measurement board becomes concrete compliance infrastructure. Each of the14 axes maps to one or more Article 9-15 requirements. The bias/fairness axes map to Article 10 (data governance) and Article 9(3) (bias testing). The privacy axis (prv) maps to Article 10(5) (personal data protection). The detector-interop axis (det) maps to Article 15(1) (accuracy metrics). The care axis maps to Article 9(2)(a) (identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks). Each measurement is Ed25519-signed and frozen in a manifest — a regulator can verify the signature, check the manifest timestamp, and confirm the measurement conditions. The verified measurement credential answers the conformity assessment question 'who measured this, when, and how?' with cryptographic precision rather than PDF attestation. The EU AI Act does not require provable isolation or formal verification for most high-risk systems. It requires continuous risk management with documented evidence — monitored containment in regulatory form. The Council of AI board provides the measurement substrate to satisfy these requirements at audit-grade precision.
